claims.text: The initial material is a CoCrFeNiTi elemental powder mixture.
The initial powder has no pre-existing lattice strain.
Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling generates substantial lattice strain and grain refinement in CoCrFeNiTi.
Milling produces a high density of dislocations.
Milling produces a nanocrystalline grain size below 50 nm.
Milling-induced defects and grain refinement alter the local chemical potential.
Milling-induced lattice strain lowers the energy or activation barrier for a metastable FCC/BCC solid-solution transition.
The defect-rich nanocrystalline state stabilizes an FCC/BCC solid solution over an equilibrium HCP phase.
Rapid SPS heating at 1000°C kinetically suppresses Ti-driven HCP precipitation.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch govern the phase stability of the proposed FCC/BCC transition in CoCrFeNiTi.
The synergy between milling-induced strain and rapid SPS heating allows the alloy to bypass a thermodynamic preference for HCP.
SPS at 1000°C facilitates near-theoretical densification without excessive HCP precipitation.
The proposed process will produce an alloy with greater than 98% theoretical density.
The processed alloy will have a dominant FCC/BCC solid-solution structure with negligible HCP content.
The processed alloy will have significantly higher Vickers hardness than cast CoCrFeNiTi.
Cast CoCrFeNiTi has low hardness, high porosity, and equilibrium phases including HCP because of Ti segregation.
Above 1050°C, grain-growth kinetics overcome strain-induced phase stabilization.
SPS above 1050°C causes phase decomposition or HCP precipitation.
Milling beyond 12 hours causes excessive cold welding that impedes uniform diffusion during sintering.
Vickers hardness testing at a 50 g load isolates grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.
